summary: This informational document describes the plan to move responsibility for bridging-related MIB modules from the IETF Bridge MIB Working Group to the IEEE 802.1 Working Group, which develops the bridging technology those MIBs manage.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 4663 describes a plan to move future bridge management-information-base (MIB) work from an IETF working group to IEEE 802.1, the group that develops bridge technology. It explains how existing documents would remain available and how reviewers could provide optional advice.

who maintains bridge mib modules under the plan
subtitle: The plan for moving future bridge MIB work from the IETF to IEEE 802.1.

tldr.problem: The IETF Bridge MIB Working Group maintained management modules for bridging technology developed by IEEE 802.1, and the IETF group did not plan further MIB development.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC describes directing new work to IEEE 802.1, keeping existing IETF modules unchanged, seeking authors' permission for derivative work, and offering optional IETF MIB Doctor advice.
tldr.outcome: It records a transition plan and expectations between the organizations. It does not report what happened after the plan was published.

today: RFC 4663 is an Informational document published in September 2006. It records a plan for moving bridge MIB work to IEEE 802.1 and does not state what happened after publication.

sections.title: The Transition Plan
sections.content:
RFC 4663 describes transferring responsibility for bridging-related Management Information Base (MIB) modules from the IETF Bridge MIB Working Group to the IEEE 802.1 Working Group. The named IETF documents cover bridges, Rapid Spanning Tree, traffic classes, multicast filtering, VLAN extensions and source-routing bridges.

The goal is to set clear expectations for both organizations. The RFC gives a general strategy and leaves exceptional, case-by-case matters to the relevant liaisons.
sections.plainLanguage: The RFC sets out which organization would handle future lists used to manage bridges. It also describes how the two standards groups could coordinate the change.

sections.title: Why New Work Moves to IEEE 802.1
sections.content:
IEEE 802.1 develops the bridging technology that the MIB modules manage. The RFC says new IEEE projects should include management work in their project requests when needed. It also notes that the IETF had required its own protocol working groups to develop related MIB modules.

The IETF considers it acceptable for IEEE 802.1 to lead MIB work because its subject-matter experts develop the technology. The IETF offers to review IEEE modules from an SNMP, MIB and SMI perspective when reviewers are available.
sections.plainLanguage: The group that develops bridge technology can also write the information used to manage it. The IETF offered review help while IEEE 802.1 took the lead on future work.

sections.title: New Modules and Existing Documents
sections.content:
The RFC recommends that IEEE 802.1 include MIB work in project requests and make MIB modules available in ASCII as well as in its document format. It says ASCII matters because network-management systems can import that format, while they may not import PDF. New IEEE modules can use the IEEE object-identifier branch.

The IETF cannot transfer existing documents to IEEE without the authors' consent. The plan says IEEE should seek the needed permission. Existing IETF modules would remain unchanged and be treated as frozen; new independent IEEE modules could add or update management coverage without changing the old documents.
sections.plainLanguage: IEEE 802.1 would develop new management documents, and the existing IETF documents would stay unchanged. The IEEE would need permission from the authors before adapting those documents.

sections.title: Optional MIB Doctor Review
sections.content:
The RFC describes a loose offer for IETF MIB Doctors to review IEEE 802.1 modules when an individual reviewer is available and willing. IEEE 802.1 editors and chairs decide whether to use the advice. The document recommends asking for review early and developing an IEEE review team of its own.

These reviews are not equivalent to the formal IETF MIB Doctor review process. The RFC warns against describing IEEE documents as having passed formal MIB Doctor review when comments were provided on an ad hoc basis.
sections.plainLanguage: IETF experts may offer advice when they have time, but IEEE 802.1 decides whether to use it. The RFC says this optional advice is not a formal IETF review.

sections.title: Security, IANA and Rights
sections.content:
The RFC says the transition plan does not affect security and requires no IANA action. It does discuss object-identifier registration and recommends keeping existing assignments in place to reduce disruption.

The document also explains that the IETF's rights do not allow it to authorize transfer of authors' work without their consent. It recommends that derivative work acknowledge the RFCs it builds on, while noting that the IETF cannot require that acknowledgment in agreements between authors and another organization.
sections.plainLanguage: The plan changes who does future work, not network security or identifier assignments. Authors must give permission before another organization adapts their documents.
